title: How do I choose Medicare coverage that fits my budget?

payload.title: How do I choose Medicare coverage that fits my budget?
payload.excerpt: Choosing Medicare coverage that fits your budget means comparing premiums, deductibles, coinsurance, and out-of-pocket maximums, not just the sticker price.
payload.author: David Haass
payload.imageAlt: How do I choose Medicare coverage that fits my budget?
payload.seoTitle: Choosing Medicare Coverage on a Budget | MedicareFAQ
payload.seoDescription: Learn how to compare Medicare premiums, deductibles, and out-of-pocket costs to choose coverage that truly fits your budget in 2026.

structuredSections.text: The Real Cost of Medicare Isn't Just the Premium

structuredSections.content: A $0 premium plan can end up costing more than a $150-a-month plan once you factor in copays, drug tiers, and hospital stays. This surprises a lot of people who assume the cheapest sticker price wins. Budgeting for Medicare means looking at four numbers at once: premium, deductible, coinsurance, and out-of-pocket maximum.

In 2026, the standard Part B premium is $202.90 per month, and that's just one piece of the puzzle. Add in Part A costs, a possible Part D plan, and any supplemental coverage, and your monthly number can shift significantly depending on how you structure your coverage.

structuredSections.calloutText: Part B premium: $202.90/month. Part B deductible: $283/year. Part A hospital deductible: $1,736 per benefit period. These figures reset every January and apply to nearly everyone on Original Medicare.

structuredSections.text: Medicare Terms That Actually Affect Your Wallet

structuredSections.content: Medicare terminology can feel like a second language, but a handful of words drive nearly every budgeting decision you'll make. Understanding them upfront saves you from guessing later.

items: **Premium:** the amount you pay monthly, regardless of whether you use care.
**Deductible:** what you pay out of pocket before your plan starts sharing costs.
**Coinsurance:** your percentage share of a bill after the deductible is met.
**Out-of-pocket maximum:** the most you'll pay in a year before your plan covers 100%.

structuredSections.calloutText: Original Medicare (Parts A and B) does not include an annual out-of-pocket maximum. Without a Medigap policy or Medicare Advantage plan, a serious illness could lead to costs that add up quickly with no ceiling.

structuredSections.content: Most people choose between two main routes: Original Medicare paired with a Medigap and Part D plan, or a Medicare Advantage plan that bundles everything together. Each path has a different cost pattern, and the right one depends on how you prefer to budget.

structuredSections.title: Original Medicare + Medigap vs. Medicare Advantage
rows: None on Original Medicare; Medigap limits vary by plan
Often limited to a local network
Lower monthly cost, more variable copays
structuredSections.footnote: Costs vary by carrier, plan, and state. Compare specific plan documents before enrolling.

structuredSections.content: If predictable monthly costs matter most to you, a Medigap plan paired with Part D tends to smooth out the bumps. If a lower premium is your priority and you're comfortable with a network, Medicare Advantage may fit better.

structuredSections.text: A Simple Way to Match Coverage to Your Budget

structuredSections.content: Rather than starting with plan names, start with your own numbers. This keeps the comparison grounded in what you actually need instead of what sounds appealing on paper.

items: **List your current doctors and prescriptions** so you can check network and formulary coverage before enrolling.
**Estimate your monthly budget** for healthcare, including premiums and expected copays.
**Decide how much risk you're comfortable with**; lower premiums often mean higher costs if you get sick.
**Compare at least three plans side by side** using total estimated annual cost, not just premium.
**Check for extra help programs** if your income is limited.

structuredSections.calloutTitle: Estimate Total Annual Cost, Not Monthly Cost
structuredSections.calloutText: Multiply the monthly premium by 12, then add your expected deductible and a realistic estimate of copays based on last year's doctor visits. This total gives you a far more accurate budget picture than the premium alone.

structuredSections.content: I always tell people to pull out last year's medical bills before comparing plans. Most folks guess at their healthcare usage, but your actual doctor visits and prescriptions from the past twelve months are the best predictor of next year's costs. It takes ten minutes and it changes which plan actually makes financial sense for you.

structuredSections.text: Mistakes That Quietly Raise Your Costs

structuredSections.content: A few common missteps can turn an affordable plan into an expensive one, often without the person realizing it until a bill arrives.

items: Choosing a plan based only on the premium and ignoring the deductible or copay structure
Not checking whether a preferred doctor or hospital is in-network for the year ahead
Skipping Part D enrollment when first eligible, which can trigger a **late enrollment penalty**
Missing income changes that could qualify you for lower costs through Extra Help
Assuming all Medigap plans cost the same, when pricing varies significantly by carrier and state

structuredSections.calloutText: If you go without creditable drug coverage for 63 days or more after becoming eligible, you may owe a permanent penalty added to your Part D premium. The 2026 base premium used in this calculation is $38.99, and the penalty grows the longer you wait.

structuredSections.text: How Income Affects What You Pay

structuredSections.content: Higher earners pay more for Part B and Part D through IRMAA, an income-related surcharge based on tax returns from two years prior. If your income was above certain thresholds in 2024, your 2026 premiums reflect that.

structuredSections.title: 2026 IRMAA Part B Monthly Premiums by Individual Income
structuredSections.footnote: Married couples filing jointly have separate, higher thresholds. Part D also carries an additional IRMAA surcharge ranging from $14.50 to $91.00 per month.

structuredSections.content: If your income dropped since 2024 due to retirement or another qualifying life event, you may be able to request a reduction using Social Security's IRMAA appeal process. This step is often overlooked but can meaningfully lower your monthly premium.

structuredSections.text: When to Get a Second Set of Eyes on Your Choice

structuredSections.content: Reading about Medicare and actually comparing plans against your specific doctors, prescriptions, and budget are two different tasks. Many people research for weeks and still feel unsure whether they've landed on the right plan.

A licensed Medicare agent can walk through your list of medications and providers, check them against specific plans in your area, and show you real cost estimates rather than general ranges. This isn't about being pushed into a decision; it's about getting a clear comparison built around your situation before you commit.

structuredSections.calloutText: Working with a licensed Medicare agent typically costs you nothing extra. Agents are compensated by carriers, not by charging you fees, so getting a second opinion on your plan choice doesn't add to your budget.

faqs.question: How do I know if I can figure out Medicare on my own?
faqs.answer: You can research the basics on your own, but comparing exact costs for your specific doctors and prescriptions is harder without plan-specific tools. Many people read for weeks and still want a second opinion before enrolling. There's no rush to decide alone; help is available whenever you're ready.

faqs.question: Will talking to a Medicare agent mean constant sales calls?
faqs.answer: A licensed agent's role is to explain your options clearly, not pressure you into a decision. You can ask questions at your own pace and walk away without enrolling if you're not ready. Reputable agents focus on matching coverage to your needs, not closing a sale.

faqs.question: What's the biggest budgeting mistake people make with Medicare?
faqs.answer: Choosing a plan based on the lowest premium without checking the deductible, copays, or network. A plan with a higher monthly cost sometimes ends up cheaper overall if you visit doctors often or take multiple prescriptions. Always compare total estimated annual cost, not just the monthly price.

faqs.question: Can I switch plans later if my budget changes?
faqs.answer: Yes, Medicare has specific enrollment periods each year, including the Annual Enrollment Period from October 15 to December 7, when you can change plans. Missing these windows can mean waiting until the next period, so it helps to mark the dates on your calendar.

faqs.question: How do prescriptions affect which plan fits my budget?
faqs.answer: Each Part D or Medicare Advantage plan has its own drug formulary and pricing tiers, so the same medication can cost very differently depending on the plan. Checking your specific prescriptions against a plan's formulary before enrolling can prevent unexpected costs at the pharmacy.

faqs.question: What if my income changes after I enroll?
faqs.answer: If your income drops due to retirement, loss of a spouse, or another qualifying event, you can request that Social Security reconsider your IRMAA surcharge. This can lower your Part B and Part D premiums without requiring you to switch plans.

faqs.question: Is Medicare Advantage always cheaper than Original Medicare with Medigap?
faqs.answer: Not always. Medicare Advantage often has a lower premium, but costs can add up through copays and network restrictions. Original Medicare with Medigap has higher monthly costs but more predictable spending and nationwide provider access.

faqs.question: How do I start comparing plans without feeling overwhelmed?
faqs.answer: Start with your doctors, prescriptions, and monthly budget rather than trying to understand every plan type at once. Comparing two or three plans against your specific needs is far more manageable than reviewing every option available in your area.

keyTakeaways: The 2026 standard Part B premium is $202.90 per month, with a $283 annual deductible and a $1,736 Part A hospital deductible per benefit period
Original Medicare has no annual out-of-pocket maximum, so a Medigap or Medicare Advantage plan can prevent unlimited costs during a serious illness
Medigap plus Part D offers predictable monthly costs, while Medicare Advantage often has lower premiums but requires network use
Going without creditable drug coverage for 63 days or more triggers a permanent Part D penalty on top of the 2026 base premium of $38.99
Higher earners pay IRMAA surcharges based on income from two years prior, but a life change like retirement may qualify you for a reduction
